title: Alpine Butterfly vs. Swimsuits For All: Coverage Is Not the Same as Bust Support
summary: A high-coverage one-piece can still lack the structure a fuller bust needs in water. Comparing two current suits shows when cup sizing, underwire, adjustable straps, and torso measurements deserve priority.
author: Curvy& Editorial

sections.heading: A covered bust is not necessarily a supported bust
paragraphs: A September r/PlusSizeFashion post described one shopper's experience with Alpine Butterfly's Onesie in Cherry Pie: at a reported 42DD, the suit felt insufficiently structured and secure once wet. That account is one person's result, not a general verdict on the brand. It does expose a common shopping mistake, though: reading visual coverage as evidence of bust support.

Coverage describes how much skin a neckline, back, or leg opening encloses. Support depends on how the garment controls weight and movement through features such as a shelf bra, underwire, separate cup volume, stable band tension, adjustable straps, and an appropriate torso length. A suit can cover the chest fully and still ask stretchy outer fabric to do nearly all the supporting.

sections.heading: The Onesie's current listing leaves support questions open
paragraphs: Alpine Butterfly presents the Onesie as a versatile style for swimming, working out, and wearing beyond the pool, and its current product page offers XS through 6X. The page's size chart supplies bust, waist, and hip ranges. For example, 1X is mapped to US 18–20 with a 42-to-46-inch bust, while 2X maps to US 22–24 with a 46-to-50-inch bust.

The listing does not currently specify underwire, molded cups, a shelf bra, adjustable straps, an underbust measurement, or a torso measurement. Absence from the listing does not prove that no internal detail exists, but it means a shopper should not assume bra-like engineering from the silhouette. A 42DD bra label also cannot choose an Alpine size by itself: band and cup are separate variables, while this chart groups several inches of full-bust circumference into each general apparel size.

sections.heading: The Swimsuits For All option publishes more fit controls
paragraphs: Swimsuits For All's Cup-Sized Mesh Underwire One-Piece takes a more explicit approach. Its official listing names an underwire bra, adjustable back straps, Power Mesh front lining, full lining, and cup-group choices. The current selector displays D/DD, E/F, and G/H groups across much of the offered size range, although availability varies by numbered size.

Its one-piece chart also publishes overbust, underbust, waist, hip, and torso measurements for cup-sized styles. At size 16, for instance, the underbust remains 36 inches while the listed overbust increases across D/DD, E/F, and G/H groups. That makes the suit the more informative first test when separate bust volume and band anchoring are the main priorities. It is not automatically better for every body: underwire position, cup shape, strap spacing, and torso length still have to agree with the wearer.

sections.heading: There is a size-range tradeoff, not a universal winner
paragraphs: Alpine Butterfly's chart extends through 6X, which it maps to US 36–38, with bust ranges rather than bra cups. The cited Swimsuits For All product currently displays numbered cup-sized options through 26. Shoppers above that product's range may value Alpine's broader apparel sizing, but should contact the brand for support construction and garment measurements before expecting the suit to function like a bra-sized design.

For either suit, measure full bust, snug underbust, waist, fullest hip, and torso loop from shoulder through the crotch and back to the same shoulder. If the full bust suggests a larger general size than the waist and hip, sizing up can create loose fabric elsewhere without producing a stable underbust anchor. In that case, cup sizing or a swim top sold separately from the bottom is often a more precise route than forcing one apparel size to solve every proportion.

sections.heading: Simulate the water before removing the hygiene liner
paragraphs: Try the suit dry with tags and hygiene liner intact. Reach overhead, bend, twist, and mimic a swim stroke. The neckline should return to position, the bust should not escape toward the armholes, the underwire should surround rather than sit on breast tissue, and the straps should support without carrying the entire load. Remember that swim fabric often feels less secure once saturated, so a barely adequate dry fit is not a reassuring test.

Return costs deserve the same attention as fit. Alpine Butterfly allows eligible returns within 30 days of delivery, with a $20-per-item restocking fee that is waived for store credit or exchange; sale items are final. Swimsuits For All requires eligible items to be received within 60 days of shipment and applies a $10.99 processing fee to most refunds, while eligible exchanges or gift-card returns waive that fee. Both require unworn condition, original tags, and the hygiene liner, so inspect support carefully without treating the suit as pool-ready.
bullets: Prioritize published underbust, cup, and torso information when support is the main need.
Ask what internal bust structure exists when a product page lists only full-bust circumference.
Keep tags and the hygiene liner in place during a careful dry movement test.

researchNote: This comparison uses a September 2026 community report as a question to investigate, then checks both current products, size systems, construction claims, and return policies on official pages. The community experience is individual; the conclusion that cup-specific construction offers more fit controls is an editorial judgment based on the published specifications.
